QF.id: IV Fixed Income Instruments and Bond Markets_24

question.text: Which theory of term structure suggests that long-term rates are simply the geometric average of expected short-term rates?

explanation.text: The Logic: The Pure (Unbiased) Expectations Theory holds that long-term interest rates reflect the market's collective expectation of future short-term rates. Mathematically, a long rate is built up as the geometric average of expected successive short rates over the period, so forward rates serve as unbiased predictors of future spot rates. The Trap: Liquidity Preference Theory adds a term/maturity premium on top of expectations, so long rates exceed the simple average of expected short rates. Market Segmentation Theory holds that different maturity segments are determined independently by their own supply/demand. Preferred Habitat Theory says investors have preferred maturity habitats but can be coaxed out with sufficient premium — none of these reduces long rates to a pure geometric average of expected short rates. Note: The specific naming and characterization of Pure Expectations, Liquidity Preference, Market Segmentation, and Preferred Habitat theories was not found in the cited workbook pages (NISM Series IV, pages 30-34, which cover term-structure definitions and yield-curve shapes/shifts). The framing above is standard fixed-income/term-structure theory as taught in general finance literature.
